correctness.rationale: Gauge the phases of the unilateral shift recursively along the coordinate chain. Absolute values of a trial vector suffice for the numerical radius of the resulting nonnegative shift. The two parity classes on the k+1 interval vertices are both nonempty; normalizing each to squared mass 1/2 gives the same edge product 1/(2 sqrt(mn)) and thus the upper dual bound for every starting index and arbitrary bounded ambient weights. For odd k the alternating weights give disjoint norm-one two-vertex blocks. For even k=2q the stated adjacent-weight sums at even and odd vertices are 2 sqrt(q/(q+1)) and 2 sqrt((q+1)/q), including both endpoints. They give a strictly positive eigenvector with eigenvalue one; conjugation by its diagonal makes the block row-stochastic and hence its spectral radius one. The edge sum is 2 sqrt(q(q+1)). Equality on the interval forces a common phase and equality in the top-eigenvalue Rayleigh quotient; stepping through the vertex equations from the left endpoint uniquely fixes each edge. This includes k=1 and only asserts uniqueness for weights vanishing outside the interval. The even-length improvement follows by comparing k(k+2) with (k+1)^2. These exact equations establish all lengths; the frozen numerical script is supplementary, not rerun or treated as an independent certificate.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The path representation is genuinely equivalent. Writing the adjacency matrix in bipartite blocks makes the estimate a bilinear pairing against constant left and right unit vectors. Attaining that estimate with the path zero pattern requires matching every vertex equation; the prior norm representation does not supply those edge values. A block-LMI feasibility formulation has the same optimization issue, and a Schatten radius is a different objective.
